The current reading guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability and linear algebra. Neural roles, additional stochastic/information/filtering tools and spatial-model ideas must be taught. The eye path includes Chapters1–9, so its information scaling legitimately depends on the preceding memory teaching. No prior stochastic calculus or neuroscience is assumed.

Undergraduate calculus, basic probability and linear algebra, as stated at reading-guide74. Neuroscience and the additional random-field, information and filtering ideas are not silently assumed. The two-foundations-then-place route was checked for its needed prior teaching.

passages.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ExplainerHeadings = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The subject is neuroscience: how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The three papers examine mathematical models that store a quantity such as an angle, eye movements and neural activity recorded in macaque monkeys, and location-dependent neural activity recorded in rodents and bats. [They ask how activity can retain a value, how an internal fluctuation can move the eyes, and why a cell can respond at several separate locations.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = NO --> A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears. The eyes must hold an angle while an animal looks at a target. A moving animal must keep track of where it is. These tasks depend on groups of [[**neuron**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s, the brain's signaling cells]{.definition-explanation}, whose electrical signals are brief and variable. Computational and systems neuroscience studies how these cells and their interactions support such behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions. Recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement. <!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = YES -->

Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. [Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists.]{.key-statement} The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> [Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network's current value limits how slowly that value can wander.]{.key-statement} Under the model's assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the [diffusion calculation](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html), its long-delay behavior, the [information bound](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html), and the limits of [readout](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html).[^orientation-memory] <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} It changes the image reaching the [[**retina**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye]{.definition-explanation}. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. [Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = YES -->

They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell's activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement's amplitude and time dependence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the [shared-drive inference](../chapters/ch-eye-drift.html), the [timing of drift](../chapters/ch-eye-timing.html), and the [proposed circuit mechanism](../chapters/ch-eye-circuit.html).[^orientation-eye] <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [A [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the [**hippocampus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations.]{.definition-explanation} [Each connected region of elevated activity is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. [Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = YES -->

Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the [spatial model](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html), its [size and shape predictions](../chapters/ch-place-sizes.html), and the [tests and circuit interpretation](../chapters/ch-place-tests.html). They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.[^orientation-place] <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in [Chapter 13](../chapters/ch-synthesis.html). <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

The reading path builds from the signals to the models and then their tests: <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

**Chapters 3–6:** derive memory diffusion, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and readout. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->

The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. The References section gives full source details. The original paper figures are discussed by number and can be inspected in the linked PDFs.
After the foundations, the [guide map](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) shows the three paper questions together.

On a first reading, follow the main text, figures, assumptions, and results. The expandable notes preserve longer calculations and extensions. Open one when you want to check the steps behind a result. The explanations needed for the next section remain in the main text.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> Chapters 3–6 explain [how interacting neurons can retain a value while random spike timing changes it.]{.key-statement} Their treatment of the Burak and Fiete appendix separates three parts of each substantial topic: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->

**Neural mechanism:** which cells and signals interact, what changes, and which features are assumptions of the model. For readout, this part also states what an observer can measure and which value it must estimate. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
**Mathematical derivation:** the general tool, its conditions, and the calculation after neural quantities are assigned to the symbols. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
**Interpretation:** what the result predicts about memory or readout, and what its assumptions leave unresolved.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = NO --> [An equation that specifies how a cell responds belongs to the model. A derivation works out what follows from that choice.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> For example, a spike can disturb several cells' activity. The circuit's interactions remove some changes, while others leave the represented angle displaced. Linear algebra calculates which part survives. Probability gives the spread of that displacement. The result then predicts how quickly memory errors accumulate in this model. The mathematical tools also apply to other systems, but this neural prediction depends on the circuit and spike statistics used in the calculation. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

The same distinction matters for readout. A calculation of the best possible estimate sets a benchmark under specified access to neural signals. Establishing that an animal's neurons implement the assumed computation requires separate evidence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = NO --> For a first conceptual pass, read the mechanism, inspect the displayed result and its variables, then read the interpretation. Follow the mathematical derivation when you want to understand why the result holds or calculate with it. Assumptions remain part of both readings. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> The [PNAS appendix](https://www.pnas.org/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1073%2Fpnas.1117386109&file=Appendix.pdf) supplies both neural-model choices and mathematical arguments. Throughout the guide, $D$ denotes the [[**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which sets how quickly uncertainty spreads]{.definition-explanation}. In the basic one-dimensional model, $D$ is constant, neither direction is favored, and no boundary limits the motion. Its [[**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} (MSD), the average squared change in the represented coordinate after elapsed time $t$]{.definition-explanation}, is $2Dt$. [Chapter 2](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-diffusion) explains this model and its assumptions.
The other recurring symbols are:
$d$: spatial dimension.
$\theta$: the represented coordinate in the memory chapters.
$q$: the normalized threshold in the place-field chapters, called $\theta$ in that paper.
$C$: the spatial covariance in the place-field chapters.
The copies are the published versions. Supporting information is linked separately.

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. [Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system.]{.key-statement} The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know how its activity represents that value and what makes the activity variable. We begin with the spikes that cells send and the patterns of firing rates across a population. A model of spike counts then shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. We then learn how to tell whether measurements vary together and how to separate random spreading from a change in the average value. Those distinctions will let us interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> [A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called [**spike**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} [A [**firing rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the expected number of spikes per unit time.]{.definition-explanation} A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES -->

[Neurons affect one another through connections called [**synapse**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects:
[An [**excitatory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}
[An [**inhibitory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} reduces it.]{.definition-explanation}

The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. [When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has [**recurrent connectivity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears.

[A [**tuning curve**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} gives a neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation} For eye angle $\theta$, a simple local model is $r_i(\theta)=b_i+k_i\theta$. Neuron $i$ has baseline rate $b_i$ in spikes per second and slope $k_i$ in spikes per second per degree. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.[^f-eye]
Different cells have different tuning curves. The vector

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> [is a [**population code**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: the pattern across $N$ neurons carries information about $\theta$.]{.definition-explanation} The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. [Reading a value from observed spikes is [**decoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} [Establishing a population pattern from an input is [**encoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} [The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a place cell fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a place field. One neuron can have several fields. [A [**rate map**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there.]{.definition-explanation} Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model's expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.[^f-place] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells, but their connections differ:
CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation.
CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation.

[A [**grid cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena.]{.definition-explanation} These repeated grid fields and a place cell's irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1's output maps need not identify where the animal's position estimate is maintained.[^f-anatomy]

A tuning curve describes expected activity, but a brief spike observation can differ each time the same value is represented. [The 2012 model describes this variability with a [**Poisson process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. At constant rate $r$, the number $K$ of spikes in an interval of length $\Delta t$ obeys]{.definition-explanation}
Here $\lambda$ is an expected count, so it has no units. For this distribution,

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> Summing $k\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda$. Likewise, summing $k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda^2$. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$, <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> The count variance grows with rate, while its size relative to the mean falls. Its relative standard deviation is $\sqrt\lambda/\lambda=1/\sqrt\lambda$. This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.[^f-poisson] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
<div class="publisher-worked-calculation publisher-fold-always">
[**Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population**]{#sec-foundations-count-example}

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is $20\times0.05=1$. The probability of seeing no spike is $e^{-1}=0.368$. A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation $\sqrt{20}=4.47$. A neuron that receives spikes from a memory circuit can use them to estimate the value stored by that circuit. [Collecting more spikes helps distinguish nearby activity patterns, but during collection the pattern itself keeps moving.]{.key-statement} The same variability that limits readout also perturbs the recurrent network. Burak and Fiete connect these two effects by deriving a lower bound on memory diffusion from the information in the spikes.[^p1-info-main]

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> The useful quantity is how clearly a short spike sample distinguishes nearby memory values. Comparing that quantity with the random motion already derived gives a minimum rate of memory spreading. This is a limit for a particular network, so using it to compare different networks also requires keeping track of what changes and what stays fixed. More information can permit better stability without ensuring that a particular circuit achieves it. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->

The [network projection](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value.

**Neural mechanism.** A receiving neuron gets spikes, not a label saying which angle the memory circuit represents. The same angle can produce different spike counts on different trials. To read the angle, an observer needs to know how each cell's expected count changes with angle and how much that count fluctuates when the angle stays fixed.

[[**Fisher information**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} measures how sensitively the probabilities of possible observations change when the value being estimated changes slightly.]{.definition-explanation} Here the observations are spike counts and the unknown value is the circuit's present memory coordinate $\theta$. [Information is large when a small change in the stored value changes the expected counts strongly compared with their random spread.]{.key-statement} It is a property of the spike model at a particular value of $\theta$, before choosing a rule for decoding the spikes.

“Local” means comparing values close to the current one. A neuron can distinguish small changes near one angle yet respond identically at two distant angles. Fisher information describes the nearby distinction. A large value alone does not resolve that distant ambiguity.

Let $h$ be the observation duration in seconds and $n_i$ neuron $i$'s spike count. For this calculation, hold $\theta$ effectively fixed during observation and assume positive rates. Once that state is fixed, the model treats the counts from different cells as independent Poisson variables. Their mean and variance are both $\bar r_i(\theta)h$. This is a short observation approximation to the recurrent circuit, whose state can otherwise move while spikes are collected.

Consider an illustrative neuron with rate 40 spikes per second at the angle of interest. Near that angle, each degree of change increases its rate by 20 spikes per second. For a circuit representing position, three questions arise:
**Spatial map:** What activity pattern corresponds to each position? The place-field model addresses this question.
**Memory motion:** How does the represented position evolve when there is no corrective input? The persistent-activity model addresses this question.

**Observed movement:** How does a downstream physical system transform that changing signal into an observable movement? The eye-drift model combines a candidate account of memory motion with a detailed account of this transformation.[^s-three]

The objects differ even when the word position appears in all three. In 2012, $\theta(t)$ locates a network state on its attractor. In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, $x$ locates an animal in an environment, and $h_i(x)$ is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered $x$ through time.
The [guide map](ch-persistence.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) gives a visual comparison of these three questions.

Related studies test the assumptions and ask questions the three papers leave open:

**Integrating movement:** The eye-position account begins with Seung's line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete's earlier grid-cell study examines [[**path integration**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, updating a position estimate from movement.]{.definition-explanation} In its model, velocity drives recurrent population activity, and errors accumulate in the position estimate. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.[^s-attractors]

**Storage capacity and changing synapses:** Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior. Transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.[^s-extensions]

**Recordings from larger environments:** For place fields, Eliav and colleagues' long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues' large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.[^s-place-data]
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->

**Connectivity and learning:** Gaussian spatial statistics do not identify a unique pattern of connections. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in [[**dendrite**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s, the branching input structures of neurons,]{.definition-explanation} can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model's success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.[^s-wiring] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

**Benefits for perception:** The source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.[^s-acuity]

These short definitions support lookup after the explanations and examples in the main chapters.

[[**abducens nucleus:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brainstem group containing the motor neurons recorded in the eye-drift study. Their axons activate the lateral rectus eye muscle.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**activity bump:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A localized peak of population firing rates across neurons ordered by their preferred represented values.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**attractor manifold:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The continuous family of persistent activity states, described by its represented coordinates rather than by every neural activity separately.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Betti numbers:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Counts of independent connected components, loops, cavities, and their higher-dimensional counterparts.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Brownian motion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous random process starting at zero with independent Gaussian increments of mean zero and variance equal to elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**causal filter:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A rule whose current output depends only on present and past input.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**coefficient of determination:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For the optimal linear prediction with an intercept, the fraction of response variance removed by prediction. With one predictor it equals the squared correlation.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**coefficient of variation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Standard deviation divided by mean. In the spike-train discussion it is applied to interspike intervals.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**continuous attractor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and neutral motion along it in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**convolution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An integral or sum combining past input values with a shifted response kernel to obtain a filtered output.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = NO -->

[[**correlation coefficient:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Covariance divided by the product of standard deviations, giving a dimensionless measure of linear association.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = YES -->
[[**covariance:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The mean product of two centered random variables, measuring their shared variation.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Cramér Rao bound:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A lower bound on local unbiased estimation variance under the required regularity conditions, expressed through inverse Fisher information.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**critical point:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point where a function's gradient is zero. The Euler calculation also requires invertible Hessians.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**decoding:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Estimating a represented value from neural responses.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**dendrite:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A branching input structure of a neuron.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**diffusion coefficient:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The coefficient $D$ in the local one-dimensional displacement variance $2Dt$. Its units are coordinate squared per time.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**diffusion tensor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The matrix giving local coordinate-displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Dirac delta:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point-mass distribution. In the initial-condition equation all probability is concentrated at the specified coordinate.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The change in a coordinate between two observations. For eye angle, $\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)$ over lag $\ell$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**encoding:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Establishing a population activity pattern from an input.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**estimator:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A rule that converts observed data into an estimated value. The memory decoder estimates an angle or other represented coordinate from spikes.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Euler characteristic:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The alternating sum of Betti numbers. In three dimensions, components minus independent loops plus enclosed cavities.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**excess kurtosis:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The fourth centered moment divided by the squared variance, minus three. It is zero for a Gaussian population.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**excitatory input:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the models used here, an input that increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**excursion set:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The positions where a function exceeds a specified level.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Fano factor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Spike-count variance divided by mean count, for a specified counting interval and condition.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**firing rate:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The expected number of spikes per unit time, conditional on the modeled circumstances.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Fisher information:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} How sensitively the probabilities of observations change with a small change in the value being estimated. Formally, the expected squared score. In the independent Poisson model it compares squared changes in expected counts with count variance. [Explanation and example](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi).]{.definition-explanation}
[[**fixational drift:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Slow eye motion during attempted fixation, between rapid eye movements.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**fixed point:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A state whose deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Fokker Planck equation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An equation describing how a probability density evolves under drift and diffusion. The guide states the convention before using it.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**gain:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in another.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**gamma function:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The function $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$ for $t>0$, extending factorials through $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Gaussian curvature:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For a surface in three dimensions, the product of its two principal curvatures.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Gaussian process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A distribution over functions whose values at any finite collection of positions have a joint Gaussian distribution.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**grid cell:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A spatially tuned entorhinal neuron with repeated firing fields, often approximately hexagonally arranged in a two-dimensional arena.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Hessian:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The matrix of second derivatives of a function with respect to its coordinates.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**hippocampus:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brain region involved in memory and navigation.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**hyperbolic cotangent:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The function $\coth z=1/\tanh z$, for real $z\ne0$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**hyperbolic tangent:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The function $\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})$.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**impulse response:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The output of a linear filter in response to a unit-area input impulse, from which responses to general input can be assembled.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**inhibitory input:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the models used here, an input that reduces a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**internal Fisher information rate:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The local information per unit observation time about the instantaneous attractor coordinate, as defined by the 2012 spike model.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**inverse hyperbolic tangent:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The inverse of $\tanh$ on $(-1,1)$, given by $\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Isotropy:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Invariance of the spatial probability law under rotations.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Itô convention:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A stochastic-increment convention that evaluates the noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**jointly Gaussian vector:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A random vector for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->

[[**Kac–Rice formula:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A way to compute expected crossing or critical-point counts from the joint distribution of a random function and its derivatives, under the relevant regularity assumptions.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedObject = NO -->

[[**left zero eigenvector:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A vector $v$ with $v^T A=0$. With appropriate normalization it extracts the persistent coordinate from a small state disturbance.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedObject = YES -->
[[**likelihood:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The probability or density of the observed data considered as a function of a proposed parameter value.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**linearization:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The first-order approximation to a dynamical equation near a reference state.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**lognormal distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A distribution of positive values whose logarithms are Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**low pass filter:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A filter that suppresses sufficiently rapid input changes relative to slower ones.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**mean curvature:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For a surface in three dimensions, the average of its two principal curvatures.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**mean squared displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The average squared change in a coordinate across a specified time lag.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**median filter:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A rule replacing each sampled value with a middle-ranked value from its local neighborhood. In the place maps it reduces isolated high or low rates and can change small field features.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**microsaccades:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Brief, rapid eye movements that occur during attempted fixation.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Morse theory:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A theory relating the topology of a function's level-set regions to its critical points. The guide uses a signed critical-point count under its smoothness and nondegeneracy assumptions, including boundary contributions.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**neural transfer function:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The modeled relationship between a neuron's input and its expected firing rate.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**neuron:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A signaling cell in the nervous system.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**ocular motoneurons (OMNs):**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**ocular plant:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The muscles and mechanical eye system that transform motor activity into eye motion.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**oculomotor integrator:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A neural circuit that converts movement commands into a maintained eye-position command.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**one sided t test:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A test of a mean against a reference value in a specified direction, using the mean difference divided by its estimated sampling uncertainty. The eye paper tests whether the mean cell correlation exceeds zero.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**p value:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Under the specified null comparison, the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme in the tested direction as the observed one.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**path integration:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Updating an estimate of position from movement.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeFires = NO -->

[[**place cell:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A spatially selective hippocampal neuron that fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeFires = YES -->
[[**place field:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A connected region of elevated spatial firing, as defined by the model or stated measurement procedure.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Poisson process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A counting process with independent increments and a deterministic constant or time-dependent event rate. Its count over an interval has equal mean and variance. In a recurrent model, conditionally Poisson instantaneous spike generation does not make complete spike trains have independent increments.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = NO -->

[[**population code:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A representation carried by the pattern of responses across neurons.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = YES -->
[[**precision:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The reciprocal of variance for a scalar Gaussian estimate.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**preferred angle:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An angle where a neuron's tuning curve peaks.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**prior distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A distribution representing knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the current data.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**rate map:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An estimate of spatial firing rate from spikes per time spent at each position.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Rayleigh distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The distribution of a positive variable that is a scaled square root of an exponential variable.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**recurrent connectivity:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Connections that feed activity back into the same neuronal population.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**renewal process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An event process with independent, identically distributed intervals under the fixed conditions being modeled.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**retina:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**right zero eigenvector:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A state-space direction $u$ satisfying $Au=0$ for the linearized dynamics.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**root mean squared displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The square root of mean squared displacement, expressed in the original coordinate's units.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**score:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The derivative of log likelihood with respect to the parameter being estimated.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**skew:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The third centered moment divided by the variance to the power $3/2$, measuring asymmetry.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Smoothness:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The existence and regularity of derivatives of a function. The crossing and peak calculations require different derivative orders.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Spearman correlation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Correlation computed after replacing observations by their ranks. It checks whether the two measured quantities tend to increase together without requiring a linear relation.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**spike:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brief electrical event emitted by a neuron.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**standard error of the mean (SEM):**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An estimate of uncertainty in a sample mean. Its interpretation depends on which observations are treated as independent, such as trials, cells, or animals.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**state:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The quantities that specify a modeled system's current condition and determine its subsequent dynamics together with future inputs and noise.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Stationarity:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the place-field model, invariance of spatial statistics under translating the map.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**stationary process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A random process whose probability law is unchanged by shifting its time or position origin. Weaker covariance-only stationarity must be specified when used.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Stratonovich convention:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A stochastic-increment convention using midpoint evaluation in the limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**sub-Poisson spiking:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Spiking with less variability than a matched Poisson reference according to the stated measure and conditions.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**superdiffusion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Mean squared displacement growing faster than linearly with lag over the range being described.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**synapse:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A connection through which one neuron influences another.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**systematic drift:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A nonzero mean velocity of the represented coordinate, distinct from random spreading.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Translation invariance:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the readout model, invariance under shifts of the represented value. It makes the readout variance independent of the cue state.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**translation symmetry:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Shifting an activity pattern along the represented coordinate leaves the network dynamics unchanged in form.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**tuning curve:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**unbiased:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Describes an estimator whose expected value equals the parameter locally under the conditions used in the estimation bound.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**upcrossing:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point where a function crosses upward through a specified threshold.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**weak fluctuation approximation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An expansion about the deterministic population dynamics in which the aggregate effects of many small spike contributions remain small.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Weibull distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A positive-variable distribution with survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**White noise:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An ideal noise input with zero covariance at unequal times and a delta-function covariance at equal times. Its integrated increments have finite variance.]{.definition-explanation}
